About me

Learning by building.

I’m Linus, a 2nd year BSIT student and web developer. I turn ideas into working websites, and I use AI tools and clear prompts to learn and build faster.

I study at St. Cecilia’s College-Cebu, Inc. I start with clean HTML and CSS, add JavaScript for life, and use Python, SQL and Excel to handle data and logic. I’m also an AI builder, so I know how to build with AI tools and get accurate, useful results from them.

My journey

  1. Started with the basicsI learned HTML and CSS and began building simple pages.
  2. Added logic and dataI picked up JavaScript, Python, SQL and Excel to make projects do more.
  3. Built a real projectI made FoodExpress, a full-stack food ordering website with real accounts and orders saved in a SQL database.

What drives me

  • Make things that work. I care more about a site that runs well than one that only looks good.
  • Keep learning. Every project teaches me a new tool, so I keep building.
  • Use AI wisely. I write clear prompts and check the results, so AI helps me think instead of thinking for me.

Projects

Things I’ve made.

FoodExpress

A full-stack food ordering website. Customers create an account, order from the menu, get a receipt, review their order history and cancel an order. Accounts and orders are stored in a real database.

What I learned
  • Designing SQL tables (orders and order items) and saving orders with a database function.
  • Adding sign up and login with Supabase Auth.
  • Protecting data with Row Level Security, so each customer sees only their own orders.
  • Building the front end with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and hosting it on Netlify.
Full-stackHTMLCSSJavaScriptSQLSupabaseRow Level Security

Enrollment System

A console-based school enrollment system with Admin, Registrar and Student roles. It handles account approval, role and status updates with input validation, and stores users, students, courses, enrollments and activity logs in an SQLite database, with hashed passwords.

What I learned
  • Separating what Admin, Registrar and Student users are allowed to do.
  • Storing data in SQLite tables with SQL instead of keeping it in memory.
  • Hashing passwords so they are never saved as plain text.

Coffee Shop Orders System

A console ordering system for a coffee shop. Staff can add a new order with the customer name, drink, price and status, view the active orders in the queue, or exit. Invalid statuses are rejected until the input is correct. Orders are saved in an SQLite database.

What I learned
  • Validating input with loops that repeat until the answer is correct.
  • Building a menu-driven program and keeping a queue of active orders.
  • Reading and fixing errors one at a time when the program misbehaved.
JavaSQLiteConsole appInput validation

Fast Food Ordering System

A console ordering program for a fast food restaurant, written in Python. The customer chooses whether to order, sees a menu of 10 items with prices in PHP, then enters an item number and a quantity to add it to the order. I built it in two versions: a modular one and an object-oriented (OOP) one.

What I learned
  • Organizing the same program two ways: separate functions and modules, then classes.
  • Keeping the menu as data and printing it as a neat table.
  • Reading the customer’s input step by step and confirming each added item.

To-Do List

A small interactive app built with plain JavaScript. You can add tasks, tick them off, delete them and clear the finished ones. It remembers your list in the browser, so it is still there after a refresh. Try the live demo yourself.

What I learned
  • Reacting to clicks and form input with JavaScript events.
  • Keeping tasks in an array and redrawing the list whenever it changes.
  • Saving data in the browser with localStorage.

    Behind the page

    How I built this site.

    This page is one HTML file with its own CSS and JavaScript. Here is how the main parts work.

    Typing effectA JavaScript timer types and deletes the words in my intro one letter at a time. It stays still if a visitor prefers less motion.
    Scroll animationsAn IntersectionObserver notices when a section enters the screen and fades it in.
    Photo viewerThe Moments photos open in an HTML dialog with previous and next buttons, and the arrow keys work too.
    Contact formNetlify Forms collects the messages. JavaScript sends the form in the background and shows a success or error note, and a hidden field blocks spam bots.
    Responsive layoutCSS grid and media queries switch the layout and the menu from desktop to phone.
    To-do listThe tasks live in a JavaScript array. Each change redraws the list and saves it with localStorage.

    Reflection: C programming

    My hardest bug.

    The problemMy C program’s output had no columns. The text came out jumbled, so the table was hard to read.
    How I found the causeI asked an AI tool for help and described what I was seeing on the screen.
    How I fixed itWith AI’s help, I learned to give each value a set width in printf, so every column lines up.
    What I learnedAI can explain a problem, but I still run the program and check the output myself until it looks right.
    /* a width on each value lines up the columns */
printf("%-6s %-15s %8s\n", "ID", "Name", "Price");
printf("%-6d %-15s %8.2f\n", 1, "Latte", 120.00);

    Example of the idea: %-15s reserves 15 characters, so the next column starts in the same place on every row.
